newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian rail head to slash costs, jobs-newspaper.
newsitem.headline: Italian rail head to slash costs, jobs-newspaper.

text.p: The head of Italy's state railway plans to slash its workforce by 30,000, lop two trillion lire ($1.19 billion) off costs and boost revenues in a bid to modernise the deficit-ridden mammoth, a newspaper said on Friday.

La Repubblica daily said Giancarlo Cimoli, managing director of Italy's Ferrovie dello Stato (FS), was preparing a corporate plan for the years 1997-2000 to head off a potential cash crunch in the coming years.
"One of the ultimate objectives is to privatise various bits of the company starting with Asa Passeggeri (passenger transport division)," the newspaper said.
No one was available immediately at FS headquarters in Rome for a comment on the report.
La Repubblica said the railway company could find itself in financial trouble as early as November this year, with the risk it might not be able to pay suppliers and employees.
FS made a loss of 2.7 trillion lire in 1996, 1.2 trillion deeper in the red than the previous year.

According to the Italian Treasury, the state transfers around 8.0 trillion lire every year to settle FS debt but Italy, desperate to reduce its budget deficit in a bid to join Europe's single currency, is looking for lasting ways to cut spending.

La Repubblica said in order to avoid financial collapse next year the FS would need 14.5 trillion lire from the Italian Treasury, "a sum which the Treasury is only prepared to stump up for a year and only if the company starts restructuring."

According to the plan, labour costs had to fall to around 8.9 trillion lire by 2000 from 10.7 trillion in 1996, while the workforce had to shrink to 90,000 from 121,000 currently, with job cuts seen in all divisions including central administration.

"There must be cost-cutting of the order of at least two trillion lire and a rise in sales of the same amount, a rise which will be realised through a packet of higher tariffs linked to new services offered to customers," the newspaper said.
Italy's rail services have been hit by a succession of strikes in the last few months as rail unions protested over contract renewals and plans to restructure rail transport.
Earlier in May rail executives reached a preliminary accord with five rail unions on renewing contracts but did not address the sticky issue of restructuring the rail giant.
The government has put forward a plan which would split FS in two by the end of 1997, with one company managing the rail lines and infrastructure and another managing rolling stock.
Cimoli, drafted in to run the FS last year after predecessor Lorenzo Necci was arrested on suspicion of corruption, has three decades of experience in public and private Italian industry.
In a recent interview with Il Sole financial daily he said the new contract agreement with unions would help cut costs and left the way open to modernising the rail mammoth.
He said increased labour flexibility and speeding up investment to increase automation on thousands of kilometres of track were crucial to modernisation.
"But above all we have to increase revenues by around 40 percent in the four year period in the three fundamental sectors of passengers, goods and metropolitan transport," he said.
This would involve prices rising by around 15 to 20 percent in the four year period but with special deals which would result in fuller trains, he said.
